submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective detector for the head word of a hedged scalar relation - the preposition, particle, comparative or small-amount noun that states how far something sits from a reference point - and it fires strongly only when that word is immediately preceded by a small-degree downtoner: 'just under/over/past/before/after/outside/inside/beyond/above/below/behind/ahead/up/off/short of/shy of/left of/right of/south of', 'a little more/less/lower', 'slightly off/below', 'a bit behind', 'shortly before', 'a small/slight/tiny chance', 'a little bit/something' (measured peaks 4.5-14.3, e.g. 'just under' 13.6 and 'a little more' 6.5 against 'under' 1.2 and 'more' 0.0 with no left modifier). The same relational head after an intensifier instead of a downtoner ('very', 'well', 'much', 'a lot', 'far'), after a non-small approximator ('about', 'almost', 'nearly', 'roughly', 'exactly'), with no left modifier, or after the same downtoner in front of an ordinary noun ('a little dog/cake/water') stays at 0.0-3.1, and 'just' plus a non-relational word ('just the/a/want/like/because/thinking') is inert, while a preceding measure phrase ('nine miles east of', 'three hours after', 'two feet under') gives the same head-word peak at a weaker 1.5-3.8 and colon clock times ('3:05', '1:31', '2:03') are a further weaker offshoot (2.5-6.3 on the last digit, with plain numbers like '199'/'305'/'1990' silent).

The case of the vanished sword

By
washingtonpost.com editors

By John Lockwood
Washington

One of our memorials is missing a sword.

The General Sherman memorial just south of the Treasury Building shows General William Tecumseh Sherman on horseback atop a 32-foot pedestal guarded at each ground-level corner by a soldier. The memorial was designed by a Danish sculptor named Carl Rohl-Smith. It was dedicated on Oct. 15, 1903.

The northwest soldier is an infantryman, holding his rifle by the barrel, with the butt resting on the ground. The southwest soldier is an engineer, holding his rifle in the same position. He also carries a cylinder or tube, about 3 feet long. Perhaps it contains surveying instruments. The southeast soldier is a cavalryman, with sword pointed upward across his left shoulder. At the northeast is an artilleryman — whose hands close upon empty air.

When I saw the northeast soldier, the question arose: Is he missing a rifle or a sword? Well, what would one of my heroes, Sherlock Holmes, do? Look for a cartridge box, or a scabbard.
There was a scabbard there, an empty one. So it was indeed a missing sword — a fact later verified in The Post’s Oct. 16, 1903, edition, which included a drawing showing the soldier with a sword, its point touching the ground.

The lost sword is probably rusting in somebody’s attic or slowly corroding in a landfill. I doubt even Holmes could find it now.

It happened inside a shelter for men with alcohol, drug and mental health problems at 149 W. 132nd St., which is run by the nonprofit Bowery Residents Committee.

Police said the two men got into a dispute in their fifth-floor apartment using kitchen knives, CBS2’s Brian Conybeare reported.

Police say the two roommates pulled out kitchen knives during a dipute. A 44-year-old was killed, and a 39-year-old was critically injured. No charges had been filed as of Friday evening.

“I heard something go boom,” the man said, adding that he does not feel safe in the shelter.

“We try to cope as much as we can with that,” Fabba said.

Dorsomedial hypothalamic lesions alter intake of an imbalanced amino acid diet in rats.
Within 3 h of ingesting an imbalanced amino acid diet (IAAD), rats show attenuated intake. The associated conditioned taste aversion can be ameliorated by giving the serotonin3 receptor blocker, tropisetron (TROP). A recent c-fos study indicated that the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMN) may be activated 2-3 h after ingestion of IAAD. In Experiment 1, DMN-lesioned rats (DMNL) or sham-operated (SHAM) rats were injected with saline (SAL) or TROP just before introduction of IAAD. By 3 h, SAL-DMNL rats consumed more (P < 0.01) of the IAAD than did the SAL-SHAM rats. Thereafter, over the next 21 h, the intake of the SAL-DMNL group returned to control levels. TROP treatment enhanced the intake of the treated groups; the TROP and the lesion effect were additive (P < 0.01). By d 4 of receiving the IAAD, the DMNL groups were eating less than SHAM rats (P < 0.05). The data suggest that the DMN may be involved in the early detection of the amino acid deficiency induced by IAAD, is not involved in the TROP effect and is necessary for proper long-term adaptation to an IAAD.

Risk factors for conversion to laparotomy during laparoscopic management of an ectopic pregnancy.
To identify risk factors for conversion to laparotomy during laparoscopic management of ectopic pregnancy. A retrospective chart review of patients who underwent laparoscopy for treatment of ectopic pregnancy, during a 32-month period (6/1999-2/2002), at the University of Miami Jackson Memorial Hospital. We identified 229 patients; 201 had a successful laparoscopy (non-converted group) and 28 who were converted to laparotomy (converted group). Variables analyzed between the two groups were demographic data, patient-related risk factors available to the surgeon prior to the surgery (previous laparotomy, previous laparoscopy, history of PID, history of endometriosis, diameter of ectopic pregnancy as measured by ultrasound, amount of free fluid on ultrasound, BMI), and surgeons' experience. Out of the 229 laparoscopies, 28 were converted to laparotomy (12.2%). The rate of conversion was significantly higher for less experienced compared to experienced surgeon (OR = 6.1, 95% CI = 2.35-15.88). Significantly more women had a BMI > 30 kg/m2 in the converted group compared to the non-converted group (42% vs. 14%; OR = 4.28, 95% CI = 1.7-10.75) and the converted group had significantly higher rate of large free fluid reported on ultrasound compared to the non-converted group (21.42% vs. 7.46%; OR = 3.38, 95% CI = 1.04-10.61). Less experienced surgeon, BMI > 30 kg/m2, and large amount of free fluid on ultrasound increase the risk of conversion to laparotomy during laparoscopic management of ectopic pregnancy.

Q:

Where to get flight dynamics for a flight sim model?

Once, a while ago, I tried to create a Flight Simulator X model for an aircraft that I wanted a model of, but was soon overwhelmed by having to guess so much of the flight dynamics. Is there somewhere where I could get detailed information about the flight dynamics of aircraft without contacting the manufacturer, a pilot, or having the plane itself to run tests on? I mean for things like drag at different mach, drag coefficient created by the landing gear, lift coefficient created by the flaps, detailed stuff about the engines, etc.

A:

Unfortunately I have no experience with how FSX models aircraft, but at a guess, it's model requires extensive experimental data from a real aircraft to truly get the right parameters.
And that's something no hobbyist is likely to be able to do. For that matter, it's pretty difficult for a pilot to do, since actually recording the relevant data is difficult, and some of what you need to know requires doing things with the aircraft you probably shouldn't do in most circumstances.
X-Plane's flight model and aircraft creation tool is far more forgiving. You still end up having to guess a lot of parameters, but they are generally less critical to basic handling.
All you really need to get a decent flight model out of X-Plane is a good set of reverence pictures, an eye for detail (so your model matches the geometry properly), and ideally the correct airfoil profiles and engine specifications.
(Primarily the thrust and power)
For the most part, good reference models and diagrams, and the information you'd find in the Pilot's operating handbook is enough to create a decent flight model in X-Plane.
It certainly won't be perfect, and you'll probably have to tune it, but it's a much easier task than getting that data needed for an FSX model.
I have the good fortune of being a student pilot, and as such I decided to attempt a model in X-Plane, and found that while it was far from perfect, (and needs a lot of improvement to be a 'good') model, it's behaviour was much closer to the real aircraft that I fly regularly than I was ever expecting given how much I had to guess.
I had to guess everything from the aileron deflection angles to the propeller geometry, wing airfoil choices and more, and still the resulting model was only slightly off from the real thing insofar as I know how the real aircraft flies.
I guess that's not

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The Millbrook Borough Council met for nearly three hours on Tuesday night before voting to table the proposed rezoning of the old Fairfield warehouse site. The measure, which would have allowed a developer to convert the twelve-acre parcel into a mix of light industrial space and apartments, drew more than forty residents to the chamber; several of them waited in the corridor because the fire code limits occupancy at thirty-eight.

Councilman Dale Whitmore opened the session by reading a letter from the county planning office, which had flagged concerns about storm-water runoff along the eastern edge of the property. The letter noted that the parcel drains toward the creek on its southern boundary and that the county engineer wanted a revised study before the application moved forward.

Public comment ran for an hour and twenty minutes. Most speakers opposed the project, citing traffic on Route 9 and the loss of the wooded buffer that separates the warehouse from the neighborhood on the north side. A smaller group, mostly tradespeople who said they had been laid off when the paper mill closed, argued that the borough needs the construction jobs and the tax revenue.

"You cannot keep saying no to everything and then wonder why nobody wants to invest here," said Ray Ostrander, a plumber who has lived in Millbrook since 1988. "I have watched this town shrink for thirty years. In the past we had three grocery stores; now we have one, and it is a dollar store."

Council president Anita Reyes reminded the room that the planning board had already recommended denial and that the vote on Tuesday concerned only whether to keep the application alive. After forty minutes of discussion, the motion to table passed five to two, with Whitmore and one other member opposed.

Under the current ordinance, the parcel is zoned for light industrial use, and any change requires a traffic study and a public hearing at least thirty days before a final vote. The developer's attorney, who spoke last, asked the council for a chance to revise the drainage plan and return next month.

"We are not asking for a rubber stamp," he said. "We are asking for a chance to answer the engineers' questions with actual numbers." The council agreed to place the revised application on the agenda for the first meeting in March, provided the developer submits the drainage study at least ten business days in advance.

Outside, after the vote, a handful of neighbors stood in the parking lot arguing about what to do next. One suggested attending the planning board meeting in force; another said the process was rigged and that the council had made up its mind before the hearing began. Two of the younger residents left before the conversation ended, and the rest drifted off toward Route 9.

The borough clerk said the minutes would be posted on the municipal website within five business days, and that residents who wanted to comment on the revised plan could do so in writing up to forty-eight hours before the March meeting, with copies sent to every member of the council.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Cedar Ridge Loop: A Trail Guide

Parking for Cedar Ridge is limited to the gravel lot on the east side of Route 27, and on weekends it fills by eight thirty. From the lot, follow the blue blazes north through a stand of second-growth hemlock. The first half mile is gentle and wide, and it doubles as the access path for the fire tower crew, so you may meet a utility truck coming the other way.

At the fork, ignore the yellow-blazed connector that drops toward the creek and stay on blue. The climb begins in earnest here: over the next mile the trail gains roughly eight hundred feet, switchbacking through oak and hickory before it straightens out on the shoulder of the ridge.

Around mile three the woods open up and the walking gets easier. Keep an eye on the white pines on your right; the largest of them is said to be older than the county itself, and the ground beneath it is usually carpeted with needles. This is a good place to stop for water, because the next stretch is exposed and hot in July.

The ridge itself is a slab of granite that runs for nearly a mile, with views west toward the reservoir and, on a clear day, the water tower at Halstead. Wind is constant up here, and the granite can be slick when it rains, so watch your footing near the edges.

The side trail to the overlook begins just past the old ranger station, a shingled hut that has been boarded up since the county moved its fire crews into the valley. The spur is short but steep, and the platform at the end holds maybe six people comfortably.

From the overlook, retrace your steps to the main loop and continue north. The descent is gentler than the climb and passes a series of small cascades that are worth a stop in spring. About a mile from the end you will cross a footbridge and pick up the yellow connector again, which returns you to the gravel lot.

The loop is maintained by a volunteer crew that clears blowdowns every spring; if you find a tree across the trail, report it at the kiosk rather than trying to climb over it.

Bring more water than you think you need, especially in August. Cell service is unreliable past the first mile, and the nearest ranger station is in Halstead, twenty minutes away by car. Dogs are welcome on a leash, and the loop is usually quiet on weekday mornings.

explanation_scores.explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective detector for the head word of a hedged scalar relation - the preposition, particle, comparative or small-amount noun that states how far something sits from a reference point - and it fires strongly only when that word is immediately preceded by a small-degree downtoner: 'just under/over/past/before/after/outside/inside/beyond/above/below/behind/ahead/up/off/short of/shy of/left of/right of/south of', 'a little more/less/lower', 'slightly off/below', 'a bit behind', 'shortly before', 'a small/slight/tiny chance', 'a little bit/something' (measured peaks 4.5-14.3, e.g. 'just under' 13.6 and 'a little more' 6.5 against 'under' 1.2 and 'more' 0.0 with no left modifier). The same relational head after an intensifier instead of a downtoner ('very', 'well', 'much', 'a lot', 'far'), after a non-small approximator ('about', 'almost', 'nearly', 'roughly', 'exactly'), with no left modifier, or after the same downtoner in front of an ordinary noun ('a little dog/cake/water') stays at 0.0-3.1, and 'just' plus a non-relational word ('just the/a/want/like/because/thinking') is inert, while a preceding measure phrase ('nine miles east of', 'three hours after', 'two feet under') gives the same head-word peak at a weaker 1.5-3.8 and colon clock times ('3:05', '1:31', '2:03') are a further weaker offshoot (2.5-6.3 on the last digit, with plain numbers like '199'/'305'/'1990' silent).
